newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communist probe aims to silence party-Hue.
newsitem.headline: French Communist probe aims to silence party-Hue.

text.p: French Communist chief Robert Hue said on Tuesday that he and other party leaders targeted by a corruption probe were victims of a political plot to derail a Communist revival.

Hue told France 2 television that the party had "not received a single cent" in illicit corporate kickbacks after a magistrate opened an investigation into aspects of the party's funding in the early 1990s.

He said that anti-Communists wanted to silence the party both because it campaigned against "the rule of money in French society" and because it was regaining ground as a bulwark against the far-right National Front party of Jean-Marie Le Pen.
"There is a political operation aiming to weaken this party which today is in a position to crush Le Pen in this society," he said.
He declined to say whether he believed the centre-right government, itself floundering for ways to counter Le Pen's anti-immigrant appeal, was behind the alleged plot.

The party newspaper L'Humanite confirmed that Hue, his predecessor Georges Marchais, party treasurer Pierre Sotura and L'Humanite editor Richard Beninger were formally placed under investigation for alleged influence-peddling last week.
The news was only published on Monday night.
France has been rocked by a string of political funding scandals in recent years, touching all mainstream parties. But none has reached so high into a party's leadership.

Hue said the allegations were aimed at damaging the party after a Communist finished ahead of a National Front candidate on the first round of a by-election to replace bankrupt businessman Bernard Tapie in southern France at the weekend.
Communist Roger Mei will contest the seat against National Front candidate Damien Barriler in run-off on Sunday.

Hue also said the Communists' opponents "cannot stand this party criticising the idea of money as king in French society." The Communist party is staunchly against plans for a single European currency.

Justice sources said the probe centred on suspected bribes or kickbacks paid to the party by the French utilities giant Compagnie Generale des Eaux (CGE) in 1992-1994 in connection with the award of water contracts in some 70 mainly leftist towns.

L'Humanite said the probe was looking at commercial activities linked to the party's annual "Fete de l'Humanite" festival. The step of formally opening an investigation could lead to a trial but does not imply guilt.
Magistrate Laurence Vichnievsky had searched Communist Party headquarters in June as part of a probe of nearly 13 million francs ($2.5 million) in suspicious billing by the CGE.

In May, four former managers of the private consulting firm Sicopar, a subsidiary of the Gifco group, were placed under investigation in connection with the case on suspicion of acting as middlemen. Gifco was dissolved in 1994.
